title: Windows Server LBFO Team or Active-Member Degradation
exclusions: This use case evaluates periodic `Get-NetLbfoTeam` and `Get-NetLbfoTeamMember` snapshots only for classic Windows Server Load Balancing and Failover (LBFO) teams. It reports a team whose normalized `team_status` is not `up`, or a member configured with `AdministrativeMode=Active` whose `OperationalStatus` is not `Active`. A configured standby member is not a failure merely because it is not active. The rule does not detect Switch Embedded Teaming (SET), Hyper-V virtual-switch teams, vendor-specific NIC teaming, guest NIC redundancy, switch-port/LACP state, physical cabling, packet loss, throughput imbalance, driver/firmware defects, or failovers that begin and recover entirely between five-minute samples. Microsoft states that Windows Server 2025 Hyper-V virtual switches cannot bind to LBFO and must use SET; such hosts need a separate `Get-VMSwitchTeam` design. A degraded snapshot identifies observed LBFO state, not root cause or application outage. The SPL applies no exception lookup or automated adapter/team changes and makes no regulatory, production-validation, or availability-assurance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the approved LBFO host/team/member inventory; owner and expected administrative mode for every member; Windows and NetLbfo module versions; the version-controlled `Get-LbfoHealth.ps1` collector and hash; its effective `[powershell://LBFOHealth]` input, execution identity, schedule, and source-type/index configuration; manifest and member rows sharing each `snapshot_id`; the `windows_lbfo_degraded_state` saved-search definition, ACL, dispatch history, and triggered-alert records; each result's sample time, host, team, member, team status, administrative and operational modes, failure reason, mode, algorithm, and source metadata; same-time `Get-NetLbfoTeam`, `Get-NetLbfoTeamMember`, `Get-NetAdapter`, NIC Teaming console, switch/NIC telemetry, and application reachability used for diagnosis; source-health and inventory-completeness output; bounded notification exceptions; incident disposition; and dated positive, negative, persistence, recovery, and collector-failure controls. This documentation-only review created no team, link failure, failover, Windows state, PowerShell execution, Splunk event, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest one `record_type=manifest` row and two `record_type=member` rows with the same `snapshot_id=lbfo-positive-001`, `host=win01`, `team=ProdTeam`, `team_status=Degraded`, and `member_count=2`. Member `NIC1` has `administrative_mode=Active`, `operational_status=Active`, `failure_reason=NoFailure`; member `NIC2` has `administrative_mode=Active`, `operational_status=Failed`, `failure_reason=PhysicalMediaDisconnected`. Place all rows inside the closed five-minute search window. Expect exactly one alert row for `NIC2` with `reason=team_and_active_member_degraded`, while `NIC1` is not separately returned. Repeat with `team_status=Up`, `NIC2 operational_status=Failed`, and expect `reason=active_member_degraded`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows: an `Up` team with two Active/Active members; an `Up` team with `NIC1` Active/Active and `NIC2` Standby/Standby; a member with `administrative_mode=Standby`, `operational_status=Standby`, and `failure_reason=AdministrativeDecision`; a `record_type=manifest` row with `team_count=0`; a `record_type=collector_error` row; and otherwise degraded data in the newest excluded five minutes. Also ingest a `Degraded` team with one Active/Active member and expect one team-level row with `reason=team_degraded` rather than silently treating the healthy listed member as the failed component.

dataSources: A local Windows PowerShell input runs the Microsoft NetLbfo module's `Get-NetLbfoTeam` and `Get-NetLbfoTeamMember` cmdlets every 300 seconds and emits one manifest plus one row per member. The deployment-local contract is `index=windows`, `source=powershell:lbfo-health`, `sourcetype=windows:lbfo:health`; these names are local conventions, not Splunk or Microsoft defaults. Required fields are `_time`, `host`, `schema_version`, `record_type`, `collector_status`, `snapshot_id`, `sample_epoch`, `team_count`, `member_count`, `team`, `team_status`, `teaming_mode`, `load_balancing_algorithm`, `member`, `interface_description`, `administrative_mode`, `operational_status`, `failure_reason`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. Microsoft documents the cmdlets as returning `MSFT_NetLbfoTeam` and `MSFT_NetLbfoTeamMember` objects. The collector freezes their string representations into a versioned schema and must be canary-tested after Windows changes.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1 for the supported Windows PowerShell input and deployment context, plus a local `windows_lbfo_monitor` deployment app containing the signed collector, input, parsing contract, saved search, and dashboard. The NetLbfo PowerShell module is part of supported Windows Server, not a Splunk app. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=windows source="powershell:lbfo-health" sourcetype="windows:lbfo:health" record_type="member" earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval host=lower(trim(host)), team=trim(team), member=trim(member), team_status=lower(trim(team_status)), administrative_mode=lower(trim(administrative_mode)), operational_status=lower(trim(operational_status)), failure_reason=coalesce(trim(failure_reason),"not_reported")
| where len(host)>0 AND len(team)>0 AND len(member)>0 AND (team_status!="up" OR (administrative_mode="active" AND operational_status!="active"))
| eval reason=case(team_status!="up" AND administrative_mode="active" AND operational_status!="active","team_and_active_member_degraded",team_status!="up","team_degraded",administrative_mode="active" AND operational_status!="active","active_member_degraded"), use_case="UC-1.2.52"
| stats latest(_time) as sample_time latest(sample_epoch) as sample_epoch latest(team_status) as team_status latest(administrative_mode) as administrative_mode latest(operational_status) as operational_status latest(failure_reason) as failure_reason latest(interface_description) as interface_description latest(teaming_mode) as teaming_mode latest(load_balancing_algorithm) as load_balancing_algorithm latest(reason) as reason values(snapshot_id) as snapshot_ids count as observed_rows by host team member use_case
| convert ctime(sample_time)
| table sample_time host team member team_status administrative_mode operational_status failure_reason interface_description teaming_mode load_balancing_algorithm reason observed_rows snapshot_ids use_case
| sort 0 host team member
description: Reports the latest member row from a closed five-minute LBFO snapshot when the Windows Server team status is not `Up` or an administratively Active member is not operationally `Active`. Standby/Standby members are intentionally healthy, and every result preserves the team/member state used for the decision.
value: An LBFO team can keep traffic flowing after one member fails while silently losing redundancy. Detecting that degraded state gives network and Windows teams time to repair a cable, switch port, adapter, driver, or team configuration before a second failure disconnects the server, and the exact team/member evidence prevents a planned standby from being paged as an outage.
implementation: Deploy a signed read-only PowerShell collector on each Windows Server that is approved to use classic LBFO, emit a complete manifest and member snapshot every 300 seconds, and keep LBFO and SET inventories distinct. Save the SPL as `windows_lbfo_degraded_state`, run it every five minutes over the preceding delayed closed window, and trigger on any row with a 30-minute throttle keyed by `host,team,member` plus a separate recovery workflow. Validate Up, Degraded, active-member failure, planned standby, no-team, stale-source, collector-error, and recovery states before routing to the Windows/network owner.
visualization: Build an LBFO operations dashboard with expected-host manifest freshness and collector errors first. Add single values for degraded teams and failed Active members; a host-by-team status grid using `team_status`; a member table with administrative mode, operational status, failure reason, mode, algorithm, and age; and a seven-day state timeline by `host,team,member`. Drill down to all rows for the same `snapshot_id`, then to same-time `Get-NetAdapter`, switch-port, driver/firmware, cluster/application, and reachability evidence. Label the dashboard **LBFO only** and link Hyper-V/SET hosts to their separate virtual-switch monitor so the absence of LBFO rows is not presented as healthy teaming.
schema: Versioned local PowerShell snapshot of Microsoft `MSFT_NetLbfoTeam` and `MSFT_NetLbfoTeamMember` objects
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM data model is claimed. The Change model does not represent current LBFO team/member health, planned standby semantics, snapshot completeness, or collector state. If scale requires summary acceleration, preserve one row per `snapshot_id,host,team,member` plus the matching manifest, schema version, status/mode/failure fields, expected inventory, and source-health markers; prove parity with raw snapshots before alerting.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a true mismatch to the documented snapshot policy, but the cause can be planned, transient, or incorrectly modeled.

1. **Planned NIC, cable, switch-port, or top-of-rack maintenance** — A technician can intentionally disconnect one Active member while the team remains available. Verify the exact server/team/member, switch and port, approved change, operator, start/end, application-risk acceptance, and live traffic path. Keep the degraded result as change evidence; suppress duplicate notification only with an exception keyed to `host,team,member,change_id` and exclusive UTC bounds.

2. **Dell OpenManage, HPE OneView, Lenovo XClarity, or vendor driver/firmware deployment** — Adapter firmware, driver, or management-agent work can reset a physical member and temporarily degrade LBFO. Correlate the deployment job, package version/hash, device instance, maintenance ring, reboot, Windows device/adapter state, and switch-port flap. Do not allowlist the vendor tool or all patch windows; bind any exception to the exact hosts, members, package/change, and expiry.

3. **Cluster drain, migration, or disaster-recovery exercise** — Failover Cluster, SQL Server, Hyper-V migration on older supported designs, or application DR testing can deliberately move workload before testing one link. Confirm cluster node drain state, migrated roles, test plan, reachability checks, owner, and timebox. Preserve the alert as resilience-test evidence and suppress paging only after workload drain and scope are proven.

4. **Intentional Active/Standby design** — Microsoft defines Standby as not participating until another member fails, and permits at most one standby member. A Standby/Standby row is intentionally negative. If inventory mistakenly expects every member to be Active, correct the owner-approved administrative-mode baseline; never force a standby member Active merely to clear monitoring.

5. **LACP or switch configuration convergence** — During an approved switch reload, port-channel change, or LACP timer/mode change, Windows may report a degraded team while links renegotiate. Verify both switch members, port-channel/LAG identity, VLAN/MTU configuration, team mode, approved network change, and recovery. Use a short bounded notification exception; repeated or out-of-window degradation is not planned convergence.

6. **Collector/schema defect after Windows or PowerShell change** — Missing or unexpectedly rendered `Status`, `AdministrativeMode`, or `OperationalStatus` can create misleading strings. The collector must emit `collector_error` or fail schema validation rather than substitute `up`/`active`. Compare raw cmdlet objects, schema version, script hash, and canary output. Route this to telemetry health and do not suppress it as a network false positive.

7. **Authorized failover or cable-pull control test** — A scheduled resilience test should generate a degraded result and then recovery. Match test ID, operator, exact member, workload safeguards, expected timing, and both state transitions. Retain results; suppress only duplicate operational paging after confirming the approved test.

**Safe suppression:** preserve raw manifest/member rows and the base result. Apply notification exceptions after detection through a reviewed lookup keyed to exact `host,team,member` and, where applicable, `change_id` or test ID, with owner, approver, reason, numeric `valid_from_epoch`, and exclusive `valid_until_epoch`. Reject wildcards, permanent team/member exclusions, blanket maintenance calendars, and suppression of collector errors, stale manifests, missing inventory, or nonrecovery.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Microsoft NetLbfo cmdlet, Active/Standby, and Windows Server 2025 LBFO/Hyper-V scope documentation plus Splunk Windows PowerShell input and Microsoft Windows add-on documentation; object-property strings, collector execution, LBFO/SET inventory, snapshots, fixtures, SPL, persistence, source health, alert delivery, failover behavior, recovery, and production response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Windows networking/Splunk/network-switch SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: The collector emits one manifest plus one row per LBFO member every five minutes, and the search scans one closed window. Cost is small, but inventory manifests and source-health checks are required so absent or failed collection cannot masquerade as healthy redundancy.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact LBFO scope

Assign Windows Server networking, physical network, Splunk collection/content, application/service, telemetry-health, and incident owners. Inventory every host expected to use classic LBFO, stable team name, team interface, physical member/interface description, switch/port/LAG, administrative mode, teaming mode, load-balancing algorithm, IP/VLAN/MTU, critical workload, maintenance authority, and retirement time. Also inventory Hyper-V hosts using SET and vendor-specific teams, but explicitly exclude them from this collector so an empty LBFO result cannot be mislabeled as healthy redundancy.

Microsoft documents the NetLbfo feature only for Windows Server 2012 and later; Windows client systems can expose cmdlets for remote management but do not provide client NIC teaming through this feature. Microsoft also documents that Windows Server 2025 Hyper-V virtual switches can no longer bind to LBFO and must use Switch Embedded Teaming. LBFO remains supported for other non-Hyper-V scenarios. Before rollout, classify every team as classic LBFO, SET, vendor team, or unsupported/retiring. Do not create LBFO on a modern Hyper-V host merely to satisfy this UC.

Run the collector locally through a Splunk Universal Forwarder Windows PowerShell input. The service identity needs sufficient read access to execute `Get-NetLbfoTeam` and `Get-NetLbfoTeamMember`; it needs no permission to create/remove teams, change modes, enable/disable adapters, modify routes, or configure switches. The Splunk role needs read access to the local `windows` index and saved-search scheduling permission. Separate exception approval from collector and content administration.

The detection contract is current state, not event IDs. Microsoft documents the cmdlets and object classes, but does not provide a stable public mapping for the legacy event IDs and `TeamName`/`MemberName` fields previously claimed by this UC. The collector therefore freezes selected object properties into `schema_version=1`. `team_status` comes from `MSFT_NetLbfoTeam.Status`; `administrative_mode`, `operational_status`, and `failure_reason` come from each `MSFT_NetLbfoTeamMember`. Validate the exact strings on every supported Windows build. Never convert a null/unknown property to `up`, `active`, or `NoFailure`.

Microsoft's administrative-mode semantics matter: Active permits participation; Standby does not participate until another member fails; at most one member can be Standby. The SPL alerts when the team is not Up or an **administratively Active** member is not operationally Active. It does not alert on Standby/Standby. This policy detects loss of redundancy without declaring a planned standby defective. Five-minute snapshots can miss a shorter flap; event logs, switch telemetry, and adapter counters remain supporting sources.

## Step 1 — Deploy the versioned collector and complete snapshots

Store the reviewed `scriptExample` as `windows_lbfo_monitor/bin/Get-LbfoHealth.ps1`, sign it according to local script policy, and hash/version it. It performs read-only queries, materializes all teams and members, emits one manifest for every successful run—including `team_count=0`—then emits one member row per team member. Every row shares `snapshot_id` and `sample_epoch`. It emits a separate `collector_error` row and exits nonzero if either cmdlet fails. Do not catch an error and emit an empty successful manifest.

Configure the supported Splunk Windows PowerShell input in the local deployment app rather than the add-on's `default` directory:

```ini
[powershell://LBFOHealth]
script = & "$SplunkHome\etc\apps\windows_lbfo_monitor\bin\Get-LbfoHealth.ps1"
schedule = 300
disabled = 0
index = windows
sourcetype = windows:lbfo:health
```

Confirm the installed Splunk version's exact PowerShell input syntax with the cited documentation and effective `btool` output. The script supplies `SplunkIndex`, `SplunkSource`, `SplunkSourceType`, `SplunkHost`, and epoch `SplunkTime`; verify that indexed metadata is exactly `index=windows`, `source=powershell:lbfo-health`, `sourcetype=windows:lbfo:health`, and the originating server. Avoid duplicate input deployment. Restrict script directory ACLs, deployment-app write access, and output permissions.

On a canary, inspect the raw cmdlet objects and collector output:

```powershell
Get-NetLbfoTeam | Format-List *
Get-NetLbfoTeamMember | Format-List *
```

Compare team/name/status/mode/algorithm and every member/name/description/admin/operational/failure field. Confirm one manifest, exact team/member counts, no duplicate keys, consistent snapshot ID/time, and no null decision fields. A host with no teams must emit a successful zero-count manifest; a host expected to have teams but reporting zero is an inventory exception, not a detector result.

Create companion source-health searches for: expected host with no manifest in 15 minutes; `collector_error`; unknown schema version; duplicate manifest; incomplete snapshot where observed member rows differ from manifest count; duplicate `host,team,member` in one snapshot; missing decision fields; future/old sample time; script hash/version drift; and expected-team inventory mismatch. Alert collection owners separately from network-state results.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the degraded-state search

Save the SPL as `windows_lbfo_degraded_state`. Schedule it every five minutes and trigger when result count is greater than zero. At 12:15, `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` evaluates the closed 12:05–12:10 interval, leaving five minutes for collection and forwarding. Measure delay and move both bounds together if necessary. Throttle duplicate notification for 30 minutes by exact `host,team,member`; do not suppress the base result. Implement a recovery search that requires a later complete snapshot with `team_status=up` and, for Active members, `operational_status=active` before closing an incident.

The base predicate accepts only member records from the exact local index/source/source type. It normalizes state strings to lowercase and requires nonempty host/team/member identity. The fault expression has two branches: team not Up, or Active member not operationally Active. The `reason` field distinguishes simultaneous team/member degradation, team-level degradation where the listed member appears healthy, and active-member-only degradation.

`stats latest()` collapses repeated rows for the same host/team/member inside the closed window while preserving observed row count and snapshot IDs. It does not hide multiple snapshots; `observed_rows` and `snapshot_ids` expose them. Source-health must prove the latest snapshot is complete before an alert is considered trustworthy. Do not raise the window to 24 hours, because stale degraded rows would remain after recovery.

No CIM search is supplied. `Change.All_Changes` is semantically wrong: this is a current health snapshot, not a configuration-change event. Do not map member state into a generic process, inventory, or network-session dataset merely to use `tstats`. If a summary is introduced, preserve manifests and member-grain state.

## Step 3 — Validate state, standby, persistence, and recovery

Use isolated indexed fixtures first. Assert one result for the documented degraded team/member fixture and all exact columns. Test the three `reason` branches independently. Test case normalization without accepting blanks. Test multiple snapshots in one window and confirm the latest fields and visible snapshot IDs. Test boundary times exactly at earliest and latest; Splunk's latest bound is exclusive.

Run every negative separately. Up plus Active/Active is healthy. Up plus Active/Active and Standby/Standby is healthy. AdministrativeDecision on a configured standby must not be treated as failure. Manifest, error, and zero-team records do not enter the fault search; they must enter companion health/inventory logic. Test missing team/member/state, unknown state strings, duplicate rows, incomplete manifest, late data, and a host unexpectedly disappearing.

On a nonproduction LBFO server with workload safeguards and network-owner approval, capture a baseline complete snapshot. Exercise a supported planned member transition or controlled link test according to the organization's network test plan; do not pull a production cable ad hoc. Verify `Get-NetLbfoTeam`, `Get-NetLbfoTeamMember`, NIC Teaming console, and collector agree on team/member state. Confirm a degraded result, continued application reachability where expected, alert delivery, throttle behavior, then restored Up/Active state and recovery. Test an intentional standby separately and prove no page.

Correlate with `Get-NetAdapter`, switch-port/LACP state, driver/firmware/PNP events, cluster/application movement, packet loss, and client-path checks. Windows LBFO state does not prove switch, route, DNS, application, or end-to-end availability. Record Windows/build, NetLbfo module, adapter model/driver/firmware, switch, forwarder/add-on/Splunk versions, script hash, fixture/test ID, exact UTC bounds, expected/actual output, search job, alert, incident, and recovery.

Measure collector duration, event count/bytes, index lag, scheduler skips, script errors, manifest completeness, duplicate deployment, and search cost. Keep `status=draft` until human Windows/network/Splunk/application owners accept scope, object strings, inventory, fixtures, safe failover test, persistence/recovery, alerting, dashboard, exceptions, and runbook.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage, response, and dashboard

Put source trust above team status. When a result fires: (1) verify the latest complete snapshot and raw cmdlet state; (2) confirm host/team/member identity and expected administrative mode; (3) identify whether the team or one Active member is degraded; (4) check approved maintenance/test/change; (5) inspect local adapter and driver/device state; (6) inspect the exact physical switch port/LAG/VLAN/MTU and cabling; (7) test application/client reachability from an independent vantage; and (8) assign the incident to Windows, network, hardware, or telemetry ownership with evidence.

A remaining LBFO path can keep service available while redundancy is lost, so route degraded state promptly without declaring a full outage. Escalate more urgently when every Active member is unavailable, team interface or critical application is unreachable, both switch paths share a failure, repeated state changes occur, or recovery fails. Correlate cluster and workload state before intervention.

Do not automatically enable/disable a NIC, change AdministrativeMode, remove/add a team member, change TeamingMode/LoadBalancingAlgorithm, restart a switch, install a driver, move a cluster role, or reboot from this result. Those actions can sever the surviving path. Follow the approved network/server runbook and preserve current configuration and traffic evidence first. Verify recovery through a later complete snapshot and independent reachability, not merely alert silence.

Review inventory and threshold policy after server provisioning/decommission, adapter/switch replacement, firmware/driver update, team-mode change, Hyper-V/SET migration, cluster redesign, maintenance, or false-negative discovery. Keep LBFO and SET dashboards separate. Retain evidence under local operational policy; the 30-day cost value is advisory, not a universal requirement.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot collector, Windows, and network failure modes

- **No rows from a host:** require a manifest. Check expected inventory, Universal Forwarder service, deployment assignment, effective `[powershell://LBFOHealth]`, script ACL/signature/execution policy, PowerShell availability, output routing, index, and time. Do not interpret silence as healthy.
- **`collector_error` appears:** inspect `error_type` and `error_message`, run both cmdlets under the actual service identity, verify NetLbfo availability and local CIM provider, and correct permissions/module/host scope. Never convert the error to a zero-team manifest.
- **Zero teams on an expected host:** compare owner inventory and `Get-NetLbfoTeam`. The team may have been removed, the host may have migrated to SET/vendor teaming, or the collector may target the wrong machine. Route as inventory/configuration drift.
- **Status fields are null or unfamiliar:** inspect `Format-List *`, Windows/module version, script schema, and raw object type. Fail schema validation and canary the new values; do not default null to healthy or use substring guesses.
- **Standby member pages:** confirm the SPL tests operational Active only when `administrative_mode=active`. Validate Microsoft Standby semantics and owner baseline. Correct parsing/policy instead of forcing configuration.
- **Team is Degraded but all listed members look Active:** confirm snapshot consistency, member count, latest data, switch mode/LACP, team interfaces, transient convergence, and raw objects. Keep `reason=team_degraded`; do not discard team state because member detail appears normal.
- **Member fails but team still says Up:** validate raw output and timing. The active-member branch intentionally reports loss of redundancy; correlate team interface traffic and subsequent snapshots before deciding severity.
- **Repeated alerts after recovery:** inspect closed-window timing, latest complete snapshot, throttling key, late events, duplicate collectors, and recovery query. Do not stretch the fault search across historical degraded rows.
- **Duplicate member rows:** compare snapshot ID, script/input deployment, host metadata, forwarder clones, and replay. One collector run should produce one member row per key.
- **Wrong host attribution:** confirm `SplunkHost=$env:COMPUTERNAME`, local execution, clone identity, and metadata overrides. Remote CIM polling needs an explicit authority/target schema and is outside this design.
- **SET or Hyper-V host has no LBFO data:** that is expected when it uses Switch Embedded Teaming. Monitor `Get-VMSwitch`/`Get-VMSwitchTeam` separately; never install or bind LBFO to a modern Hyper-V switch to populate this UC.
- **Network impact exists while LBFO is Up:** LBFO state does not measure packet loss, switch path, VLAN/MTU, routing, DNS, or application health. Use switch telemetry, adapter counters, packet/path tests, and application monitoring as separate controls.
- **Five-minute flap is missed:** add approved event/switch telemetry or reduce the collector interval after measuring cost; keep manifest semantics and avoid presenting snapshot polling as continuous event detection.
grandmaExplanation: We check the network cards that work together on a Windows server. If the group or one card that should be working becomes unhealthy, we warn the support team before another failure can disconnect the server.
hardware: Windows Server 2012 or later systems using classic in-box LBFO teams outside unsupported Hyper-V binding scenarios. The NetLbfo module is not an implementation surface for Windows client NIC teaming. Windows Server 2025 continues LBFO for non-Hyper-V scenarios but removes LBFO binding for Hyper-V virtual switches; use a separate SET monitor there.
scriptExample:
```powershell
# Get-LbfoHealth.ps1 -- read-only LBFO snapshot for a Splunk powershell:// input
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
$schemaVersion = 1
$sampleEpoch = [DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds()
$snapshotId = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString()
$source = 'powershell:lbfo-health'
$sourceType = 'windows:lbfo:health'
$index = 'windows'

try {
    $teams = @(Get-NetLbfoTeam -ErrorAction Stop)
    $memberSets = @{}
    $totalMembers = 0
    foreach ($team in $teams) {
        $members = @(Get-NetLbfoTeamMember -Team $team.Name -ErrorAction Stop)
        $memberSets[[string]$team.Name] = $members
        $totalMembers += $members.Count
    }

    [pscustomobject][ordered]@{
        SplunkIndex=$index; SplunkSource=$source; SplunkSourceType=$sourceType
        SplunkHost=$env:COMPUTERNAME; SplunkTime=$sampleEpoch
        schema_version=$schemaVersion; record_type='manifest'; collector_status='ok'
        snapshot_id=$snapshotId; sample_epoch=$sampleEpoch
        team_count=$teams.Count; member_count=$totalMembers
    }

    foreach ($team in $teams) {
        foreach ($member in $memberSets[[string]$team.Name]) {
            [pscustomobject][ordered]@{
                SplunkIndex=$index; SplunkSource=$source; SplunkSourceType=$sourceType
                SplunkHost=$env:COMPUTERNAME; SplunkTime=$sampleEpoch
                schema_version=$schemaVersion; record_type='member'; collector_status='ok'
                snapshot_id=$snapshotId; sample_epoch=$sampleEpoch
                team_count=$teams.Count; member_count=$memberSets[[string]$team.Name].Count
                team=[string]$team.Name; team_status=[string]$team.Status
                teaming_mode=[string]$team.TeamingMode
                load_balancing_algorithm=[string]$team.LoadBalancingAlgorithm
                member=[string]$member.Name
                interface_description=[string]$member.InterfaceDescription
                administrative_mode=[string]$member.AdministrativeMode
                operational_status=[string]$member.OperationalStatus
                failure_reason=[string]$member.FailureReason
            }
        }
    }
}
catch {
    [pscustomobject][ordered]@{
        SplunkIndex=$index; SplunkSource=$source; SplunkSourceType=$sourceType
        SplunkHost=$env:COMPUTERNAME; SplunkTime=$sampleEpoch
        schema_version=$schemaVersion; record_type='collector_error'; collector_status='error'
        snapshot_id=$snapshotId; sample_epoch=$sampleEpoch
        error_type=$_.Exception.GetType().FullName
        error_message=$_.Exception.Message
    }
    exit 1
}
```
